newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Private capital for Asian projects strong - report.
newsitem.headline: Private capital for Asian projects strong - report.

text.p: Promising trends have emerged in China and India over the past year likely to boost private sector investment in major projects, an Asian infrastructure expert said on Tuesday.

Both countries were facing population pressures and the need for private capital to hasten economic liberalisation had been recognised at a high level, said John Bastian, head of Asia project finance at accounting firm Price Waterhouse.
Bastian, releasing the June edition of the firm's Asian Infrastructure Barometer, said private sector infrastructure continued to flourish throughout the Asia-Pacific.

Power generation projects were taking the lion's share of investment as they provided a platform for industrial development, followed a fairly uniform design and included a high proportion of material produced elsewhere, he said.
The 18-nation Asia Pacific Economic Co-operation forum (APEC) called in April for more private cash to keep developing the world's fastest growing area.
Economists estimate that A$1.5 trillion is needed for infrastructure work to cope with goods and services in the region.

Bastian said in China in the past year a non-Chinese entity had been allowed to take full ownership of a large public utility, while draft build-operate-transfer (BOT) legislation had been circulated and was expected to be finalised shortly.
India has established a joint private-public sector corporation to assist in long-term capital market development, credit enhancement and other leverage financing.
Other countries such as Indonesia, the Philippines, Malaysia and Australia continued to attract strong on-going interest, although enthusiasm had waned for Laos and Vietnam.
Bastian said it appeared private sector involvement in Asian infrastructure followed a fixed pattern, with countries in the region at different stages of the cycle.
Interest was initially sparked by economic need, leading to a wave of enthusiasm, as with Vietnam and Laos a year ago.
However, roadblocks developed as countries sought to impose their own form of development, enthusiasm waned and nothing was done, he said.
Economic reality kicked in again, a few tentative projects got off the ground, perhaps with some extra regulations, and soon the country was "open for business".
"This cycle is very true if you look at China," Bastian told a briefing.
An early wave of enthusiasm two or three years ago waned when the country imposed its own approvals process, a long time-frame for projects and other conditions.
"The Chinese have started to realise that the world market is the market they are dealing in and there isn't a private infrastructure market in China that's different."
Bastian said recent changes heralded a new era for investors keen to benefit from China's massive infrastructure needs.
